title: The Binding of Isaac (the Akedah)
lead: God's command to Abraham to offer his son as a burnt offering on a mountain in Moriah, and the angel's call that stopped the knife (Genesis 22:1–19). It is a central text in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, with its own liturgy, its own feast and its own long philosophical debate.

sections.b: Chronicles places Solomon's temple on "Mount Moriah" (2 Chronicles 3:1). The prophets reject child sacrifice outright (Jeremiah 19:5; Micah 6:7). In the New Testament, Paul's words that God "did not hold back his own Son" (Romans 8:32) echo the Greek of Genesis 22:12, 16, and the voice at Jesus' baptism, "You are my dearly loved Son" (Mark 1:11), may recall "your son ... whom you love" (Genesis 22:2). Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead (Hebrews 11:17–19), and James that his faith was completed by his deed (James 2:21–23).
sections.refs: Genesis 22:1–19; 2 Chronicles 3:1; Jeremiah 19:5; Micah 6:7; Mark 1:11; Romans 8:32; Hebrews 11:17–19; James 2:21–23

sections.b: Jews read the chapter on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, include it in the daily morning prayers, and link the shofar to the ram's horn; the Midrash made Isaac a willing adult, and medieval poems imagined him slain and raised. Christians read it in Holy Week as a figure of the cross. Muslims remember Abraham's sacrifice of his son, usually taken as Ishmael, at Eid al-Adha (Qur'an 37:99–113). Philosophers have argued over it since Kierkegaard (1843) and Kant (1798), and some modern readers, such as Lippman Bodoff and Omri Boehm, argue that Abraham was meant to refuse.
